question: A 52-year-old post-menopausal woman complains of burning and grittiness, worse in air-conditioned offices. Schirmer's I test (without anaesthesia, 5 minutes) shows 6 mm wetting bilaterally. Tear breakup time (TBUT) is 7 seconds. What is the CORRECT interpretation?

answers.text: Normal tear production; the diagnosis is evaporative dry eye only

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Schirmer's I of 6 mm is below the normal cutoff of ≥10 mm — this indicates reduced tear production (aqueous deficient component). Both aqueous deficiency AND evaporative disease are likely present.

answers.text: Aqueous deficient dry eye (Schirmer I <10 mm) combined with evaporative component (TBUT <10 seconds)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Schirmer I <10 mm = aqueous deficiency (lacrimal insufficiency). TBUT <10 seconds = evaporative dry eye (lipid layer deficiency, meibomian gland dysfunction). This patient has mixed dry eye — the most common presentation.

answers.text: Normal findings — Schirmer I of 6 mm is within accepted variation and TBUT of 7 s is normal

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Both values are abnormal. Normal Schirmer I ≥10 mm; this patient has 6 mm (reduced). Normal TBUT ≥10 seconds; 7 seconds is below the threshold. Both indicate dry eye disease.

answers.text: Evaporative dry eye only — Schirmer's test is unreliable without anaesthesia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Schirmer I (without anaesthesia) measures reflex + basal secretion and is a standard clinical test. A result of 6 mm reliably indicates aqueous deficiency regardless of the reflex component. The interpretation does not dismiss this test.

overallFeedback.feedback: Normal: Schirmer I ≥10 mm, TBUT ≥10 s. This patient fails both → mixed (aqueous deficient + evaporative) dry eye disease.
Excellent! Schirmer I <10 mm = aqueous deficient DED; TBUT <10 s = evaporative DED. Mixed DED is the commonest phenotype in clinical practice.
